items.stem: A seated patient is asked to slump the thoracolumbar spine, then flex the neck, extend the knee, and dorsiflex the ankle, while the examiner watches for reproduction of leg symptoms and releases neck flexion to see whether symptoms ease. Which test is this?
options: Slump test
Straight leg raise
Prone instability test
Modified Schober test
items.explanation: This is the slump test — a seated neurodynamic sequence that progressively loads the neural structures (spinal flexion → cervical flexion → knee extension → ankle dorsiflexion). The structural differentiation step is what makes it a neurodynamic test rather than a hamstring stretch: if releasing neck flexion changes the leg symptoms, the symptoms are neural in origin.
items.pearl: The release step is the test. Without structural differentiation, you've only measured hamstring length.
items.citation: Majlesi J, Togay H, Ünalan H, Toprak S. The sensitivity and specificity of the slump and the straight leg raising tests in patients with lumbar disc herniation. J Clin Rheumatol. 2008;14(2):87-91.

items.stem: Raising the patient's UNINVOLVED leg reproduces pain down the patient's INVOLVED leg. What is this finding called?
options: Crossed (contralateral) straight leg raise
Bilateral straight leg raise
Bragard sign
A false-positive straight leg raise
items.explanation: Raising the asymptomatic leg and reproducing symptoms in the symptomatic leg is the crossed straight leg raise. It is far less sensitive than the standard SLR but considerably more specific — a positive crossed SLR is one of the stronger clinical pointers toward a disc herniation with root compression.
items.citation: van der Windt DA, et al. Physical examination for lumbar radiculopathy due to disc herniation in patients with low-back pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(2):CD007431.

items.stem: A 71-year-old reports bilateral leg heaviness and aching when walking. Which reported feature points toward NEUROGENIC rather than vascular claudication?
options: Symptoms ease with sitting or leaning forward on a shopping trolley, and cycling is tolerated well
Symptoms ease within 2–3 minutes of simply standing still
Symptoms are reproduced at a consistent, predictable walking distance every time
The legs are cool with diminished pedal pulses
items.explanation: Neurogenic claudication is posture-dependent: lumbar flexion opens the canal, so leaning on a trolley, sitting, or cycling relieves symptoms, while walking upright and extension provoke them. Vascular claudication is demand-dependent: it comes on at a reproducible distance, eases with rest in any position within a few minutes, and pairs with vascular signs. Both can coexist in this age group — check pulses regardless.
items.pearl: Ask 'can you cycle?' — flexion-tolerant walking limitation is the cleanest bedside discriminator.
items.citation: Kreiner DS, et al. An evidence-based clinical guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis (update). North American Spine Society; Spine J. 2013;13(7):734-743.

items.stem: A patient lies prone with the trunk on the table and feet resting on the floor. The examiner applies posterior-to-anterior pressure to a symptomatic segment (pain reported), then the patient lifts the legs off the floor and the pressure is repeated (pain reduced). Which test is described, and what does the reduction suggest?
options: Prone instability test — pain reduced with muscle activation suggests a stabilization-responsive presentation
Prone instability test — pain reduced confirms segmental hypermobility on imaging
Passive lumbar extension test — pain reduced rules out instability
Prone press-up test — pain reduced indicates a directional preference for extension
items.explanation: The prone instability test compares segmental PA provocation with the stabilizing musculature relaxed versus actively engaged. Pain that eases once the patient engages the trunk and hip musculature is taken as a sign the segment responds to active stabilization — it is a treatment-response indicator, not proof of radiographic instability.
items.citation: Hicks GE, Fritz JM, Delitto A, McGill SM. Preliminary development of a clinical prediction rule for determining which patients with low back pain will respond to a stabilization exercise program. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2005;86(9):1753-1762.

items.stem: Order the steps for performing a straight leg raise.
orderedOptions: Position the patient supine with the head, trunk, and pelvis neutral, and explain what you will do
Passively raise the symptomatic leg with the knee extended and the hip in neutral rotation
Stop at the point the patient's familiar leg symptoms are reproduced and note the angle
Lower slightly below the symptomatic angle, then add ankle dorsiflexion or cervical flexion to differentiate neural from musculotendinous origin
items.explanation: Standardise the position first: hip rotation, pelvic tilt, and trunk position all change the angle at which symptoms appear. Raise until FAMILIAR symptoms appear — posterior thigh tightness is not a positive. The sensitising manoeuvre at the end is what separates neural mechanosensitivity from hamstring tension.
items.citation: van der Windt DA, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(2):CD007431 (test description and accuracy).

items.stem: Order the components of the slump test.
orderedOptions: Seat the patient upright at the edge of the plinth with the hands behind the back
Ask the patient to slump the thoracic and lumbar spine while you maintain the sacrum vertical
Add cervical flexion and hold it
Actively or passively extend the knee, then add ankle dorsiflexion
Release cervical flexion and ask whether the leg symptoms change
items.explanation: Load the neural system from the top down, then differentiate. Holding the sacrum vertical stops the patient escaping into posterior pelvic tilt. Releasing neck flexion at the end is the differentiation step — leg symptoms that ease when the neck is released implicate neural tissue rather than hamstring.
items.citation: Majlesi J, et al. J Clin Rheumatol. 2008;14(2):87-91 (test procedure and accuracy).

items.stem: Order the steps for the modified Schober measurement of lumbar flexion.
orderedOptions: With the patient standing, mark the midline at the level of the posterior superior iliac spines
Mark a second point 10 cm above and a third 5 cm below that landmark
Ask the patient to bend forward as far as comfortable, keeping the knees straight
Measure the new distance between the upper and lower marks
Subtract the original 15 cm to report the increase in lumbar flexion
items.explanation: The modified Schober uses a 15 cm span (10 above, 5 below the PSIS line) and reports the INCREASE on flexion, not the absolute distance. It is a segmental measure of lumbar mobility that deliberately excludes hip flexion — which is precisely why fingertip-to-floor distance is not interchangeable with it.
items.pearl: Fingertip-to-floor measures the whole kinetic chain. Schober measures the lumbar spine. Don't swap them between visits.
items.citation: Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 6th ed. Elsevier Saunders; 2014 (modified Schober procedure).

items.stem: A patient reports leg pain below the knee with suspected lumbar radiculopathy. Order a sensible lower-quarter neurological screen.
orderedOptions: Ask about bladder, bowel, and saddle sensation to screen for cauda equina before proceeding
Test dermatomal light touch sensation and compare sides
Test key myotomes, comparing sides for weakness
Test the patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes
Perform neurodynamic testing (SLR or slump) to assess mechanosensitivity
items.explanation: Screen for the emergency first — cauda equina questions cost fifteen seconds and change the entire disposition. Then work from least to most provocative: sensation, then strength, then reflexes, and only then the neurodynamic tests, which are the most likely to flare symptoms and can confound the rest of the exam if done early.
items.citation: George SZ, et al. Interventions for the management of acute and chronic low back pain: clinical practice guideline. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2021;51(11):CPG1-CPG60.

items.stem: In the Cochrane review of physical examination for lumbar radiculopathy, the straight leg raise showed pooled sensitivity ~0.92 but pooled specificity of only ~0.28 in surgical populations. What is the practical implication?
options: It is a reasonable rule-out test in high-prevalence settings, but a positive result alone means very little
A positive SLR confirms disc herniation with root compression
The test should be abandoned in favour of imaging
It is highly specific, so it is best used to confirm the diagnosis
items.explanation: Sensitivity ~92% with specificity ~28% describes a test that is positive in most people WITH the condition and also in most people without it. So a negative SLR is informative (few herniations are missed), while a positive one barely shifts probability. Note the studies were done in surgical populations with 58–98% prevalence — accuracy in a primary care caseload will differ.
items.pearl: SnNout applies here: high sensitivity, negative result, rules out. Just don't run it backwards.
items.citation: van der Windt DA, Simons E, Riphagen II, et al. Physical examination for lumbar radiculopathy due to disc herniation in patients with low-back pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(2):CD007431.

items.stem: How do the standard and crossed straight leg raise differ in diagnostic profile?
options: Standard SLR: high sensitivity, low specificity. Crossed SLR: low sensitivity, high specificity
Both are highly sensitive screening tests
Standard SLR is the more specific of the two
Both are highly specific confirmatory tests
items.explanation: They are complementary opposites, which is exactly why you perform both. The standard SLR screens (few true herniations escape it); the crossed SLR confirms (it is rarely positive without significant nerve root compression, though it misses many cases). Reported estimates come largely from surgical populations with high disease prevalence.
items.citation: van der Windt DA, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(2):CD007431.
items.contestedNote: Pooled specificity estimates for the standard SLR vary widely between studies (reported range roughly 0.10–1.00), and nearly all data come from high-prevalence surgical cohorts, so accuracy in primary care is genuinely uncertain.

items.stem: Majlesi et al. compared the slump and straight leg raise in patients with MRI-confirmed lumbar disc herniation, reporting slump Sn 0.84 / Sp 0.83 and SLR Sn 0.52 / Sp 0.89. What follows clinically?
options: The slump was the better screening test here, while the SLR was slightly better at confirming
The slump should replace the SLR entirely
The SLR is the better screen because it is more specific
The two tests are interchangeable
items.explanation: In this sample the slump caught more herniations (Sn 0.84 vs 0.52) while the SLR gave slightly fewer false positives (Sp 0.89 vs 0.83). Note this contradicts the Cochrane pooled figures for SLR sensitivity — different populations and reference standards produce different numbers, which is itself the lesson. Use both tests and weigh them against the history.
items.citation: Majlesi J, Togay H, Ünalan H, Toprak S. The sensitivity and specificity of the slump and the straight leg raising tests in patients with lumbar disc herniation. J Clin Rheumatol. 2008;14(2):87-91.
items.contestedNote: SLR sensitivity here (0.52) is far lower than the Cochrane pooled estimate (~0.92). The disagreement reflects different populations, reference standards, and positive criteria — no single number is authoritative.

items.stem: The two-stage treadmill test for lumbar spinal stenosis has been reported with sensitivity ~50% and specificity ~92%. How should it be used?
options: As a confirmatory test — prolonged walking tolerance on the inclined stage supports stenosis, but a normal result doesn't exclude it
As a screening test to rule out stenosis in anyone with leg pain
As a substitute for imaging in surgical planning
As a measure of cardiovascular fitness in older adults with back pain
items.explanation: Specificity ~92% with sensitivity ~50% is a confirmer's profile: patients who walk longer on the inclined (flexed) treadmill than the level one are likely to have stenosis, but half of those with stenosis won't show the pattern. It also has practical value beyond diagnosis — it quantifies walking tolerance, which is usually the patient's actual goal.
items.citation: Fritz JM, Erhard RE, Delitto A, Welch WC, Nowakowski PE. Preliminary results of the use of a two-stage treadmill test as a clinical diagnostic tool in the differential diagnosis of lumbar spinal stenosis. J Spinal Disord. 1997;10(5):410-416.

items.stem: A systematic review of red flags for cauda equina syndrome found pooled sensitivities of roughly 0.19–0.43 and specificities of roughly 0.62–0.88 against MRI. What is the correct clinical takeaway?
options: No red flag, or absence of one, is sufficient to exclude CES — clinical suspicion must drive urgent referral
A full negative red-flag screen safely excludes cauda equina syndrome
Red flags are sensitive enough to be used as a standalone screen
Saddle anaesthesia alone has near-perfect sensitivity
items.explanation: These are poor screening properties: most patients with CES will NOT report any given red flag, so a clean screen provides false reassurance. The findings are somewhat more specific than sensitive — bowel incontinence, perineal anaesthesia, and reduced anal tone are the most specific — meaning their PRESENCE matters far more than their absence. Progressive or bilateral neurological symptoms warrant urgent referral regardless of the checklist.
items.pearl: The red-flag list is a prompt to think, not a rule-out. CES is a clinical emergency diagnosed on suspicion plus MRI.
items.citation: Dionne N, Adefolarin A, Kunzelman D, et al. What is the diagnostic accuracy of red flags related to cauda equina syndrome (CES), when compared to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)? A systematic review. Musculoskelet Sci Pract. 2019;42:125-133.

items.stem: Fulfilling at least 4 of the 5 ASAS inflammatory back pain parameters gives sensitivity ~77% and specificity ~92%. Which of the following is NOT one of the five ASAS parameters?
options: Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
Age at onset ≤40 years
Improvement with exercise but not with rest
Night pain that improves on getting up
items.explanation: The five ASAS parameters are: age at onset ≤40, insidious onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, and night pain (improving on getting up). Morning stiffness — despite being the feature clinicians most associate with inflammatory back pain, and part of older criteria sets — was dropped because it proved non-specific: plenty of mechanical back pain is stiff in the morning too.
items.pearl: The discriminating question isn't 'are you stiff in the morning?' It's 'does moving help and resting not?'
items.citation: Sieper J, van der Heijde D, Landewé R, et al. New criteria for inflammatory back pain in patients with chronic back pain: a real patient exercise by experts from the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS). Ann Rheum Dis. 2009;68(6):784-788.

items.stem: A patient referred from a spinal surgical clinic with suspected L5 radiculopathy has a clearly negative SLR. Best interpretation?
options: Meaningfully lowers the probability of a herniation with root compression, though it can't exclude it
Definitively excludes lumbar radiculopathy
Tells you nothing, because the test's specificity is poor
Confirms the pain is non-organic
items.explanation: High sensitivity is what makes a negative useful: with LR− around 0.3, a pretest probability of 60% falls to roughly 30%. That's a real shift, not exclusion. The poor specificity limits what a POSITIVE tells you — it doesn't diminish the value of this negative.
items.citation: van der Windt DA, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(2):CD007431 (LR− computed from pooled Sn/Sp).

items.stem: In an outpatient clinic, a patient with 3 weeks of low back pain and vague posterior thigh ache has a positive SLR at 60°. Pretest probability of true radiculopathy is maybe 20%. What follows?
options: Barely changes anything — with LR+ ≈ 1.3 the probability rises to roughly 25%, and false positives are common
Radiculopathy is now the most likely diagnosis
Urgent imaging is indicated
The patient should be told they have a disc herniation
items.explanation: A likelihood ratio near 1 means the test result carries almost no information. Specificity of 28% means most people WITHOUT radiculopathy also test positive — hamstring tension, hip pathology, and general pain sensitivity all produce positives. Posterior thigh ache without symptoms below the knee and without neurological signs remains, on balance, unlikely to be true radiculopathy.
items.pearl: Any LR between about 0.5 and 2 is clinical noise. Know which of your tests live there.
items.citation: van der Windt DA, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(2):CD007431 (LR+ computed from pooled Sn/Sp); Bayesian conversion is standard.

items.stem: A patient meets 4 of the 5 Flynn clinical prediction rule criteria for lumbar manipulation (symptoms <16 days, no symptoms distal to the knee, FABQ-W <19, hip IR >35°, lumbar hypomobility). Reported LR+ for ≥4 criteria is 24.4. What does this mean?
options: Probability of short-term success rises from roughly 45% to about 95% — a strong reason to include manipulation
It guarantees the patient will recover fully
It identifies the cause of the patient's pain
It means manipulation is the only treatment that will work
items.explanation: The rule predicts short-term RESPONSE, not pathology and not long-term outcome: baseline success around 45% rises to roughly 95% when four or more criteria are met. Two cautions — the validation literature is mixed, and 'success' was defined as ≥50% improvement in disability over about a week, which is a modest and short horizon.
items.citation: Flynn T, Fritz J, Whitman J, et al. A clinical prediction rule for classifying patients with low back pain who demonstrate short-term improvement with spinal manipulation. Spine. 2002;27(24):2835-2843; validation in Childs JD, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2004;141(12):920-928.
items.contestedNote: Later validation attempts have not consistently reproduced the rule's performance, and some trials found no added benefit over exercise alone. Treat it as a weak prior, not a decision rule.

items.stem: During repeated-movement testing, a patient's leg pain retreats from the calf to the buttock and their back pain increases. How should this be interpreted?
options: Centralization — a favourable prognostic sign that guides the exercise direction, but not proof of a specific pathoanatomical source
The patient is deteriorating, since back pain increased
It confirms the pain is discogenic
It rules out the need for a neurological screen
items.explanation: Distal-to-proximal migration is centralization, even when central pain worsens — direction of travel matters more than intensity. It carries genuine prognostic weight and identifies a directional preference to train. What it does NOT do is confirm the disc as the source: the evidence does not support centralization as specific enough to identify discogenic pain.
items.pearl: Centralization tells you which way to load the patient. It doesn't tell you what tissue is at fault.
items.citation: Werneke M, Hart DL. Centralization phenomenon as a prognostic factor for chronic low back pain and disability. Spine. 2001;26(7):758-764; specificity caveat per Laslett M, et al. and Chevrot A, et al. Joint Bone Spine. 2007;74(5):425-427.
items.contestedNote: Centralization's prognostic value is reasonably supported; its diagnostic specificity for discogenic pain is disputed and should not be presented as established.

items.stem: A 44-year-old with 5 days of severe low back and bilateral leg pain reports new difficulty starting urination and a 'strange numb patch' when wiping. Perianal sensation seems reduced. Most appropriate action?
options: Immediate emergency referral for urgent MRI — this is a suspected cauda equina syndrome
Continue with the planned examination and review in one week
Perform an SLR and refer only if it is positive
Advise fluids and reassess bladder symptoms at the next appointment
items.explanation: Bilateral leg symptoms, urinary hesitancy, and saddle sensory change together are enough to act on. CES is a surgical emergency where delay costs bladder, bowel, and sexual function permanently — the decision threshold for referral is deliberately low, and no examination finding you can add will safely rule it out. Refer now and document the neurological findings and the time.
items.citation: Dionne N, et al. Musculoskelet Sci Pract. 2019;42:125-133 (accuracy of CES red flags); George SZ, et al. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2021;51(11):CPG1-CPG60 (referral guidance).

items.stem: A patient with 6 weeks of low back pain scores in the HIGH-risk group on the STarT Back tool. What does this most appropriately change?
options: It flags a psychologically informed, more intensive approach — high risk reflects prognosis, not severity of tissue damage
It indicates a more serious spinal pathology requiring imaging
It means manual therapy is contraindicated
It measures how much pain the patient is currently in
items.explanation: STarT Back stratifies risk of persistent disabling pain, driven largely by the psychosocial subscale (fear, catastrophizing, anxiety, depression, bothersomeness). High risk points toward combined physiotherapy with psychologically informed care — not toward imaging, and not toward the assumption that something is structurally worse.
items.citation: Hill JC, Dunn KM, Lewis M, et al. A primary care back pain screening tool: identifying patient subgroups for initial treatment. Arthritis Rheum. 2008;59(5):632-641.

items.stem: Using Fritz and Irrgang's reported MCID of 6 points for the Modified Oswestry Disability Questionnaire, a patient improves from 42% to 38% over three weeks. What can you conclude?
options: The 4-point change is below the MCID — not yet a clinically meaningful improvement
The patient has meaningfully improved
The patient has meaningfully deteriorated
The score is invalid because it did not reach zero
items.explanation: Four points falls short of the ~6-point threshold associated with patients reporting themselves meaningfully better. That is not the same as 'no progress' — it may be too early, or gains may be showing in measures the ODI doesn't capture (walking tolerance, work hours, sleep). Keep treating, re-measure, and look at the patient-specific goals alongside it.
items.citation: Fritz JM, Irrgang JJ. A comparison of a modified Oswestry Low Back Pain Disability Questionnaire and the Quebec Back Pain Disability Scale. Phys Ther. 2001;81(2):776-788.

items.stem: A recent analysis calculated the ODI's MCID sixteen different ways and got values ranging from under 1 point to over 20, averaging about 10.5. What should a clinician do with that?
options: Treat any single published MCID as method-dependent — use it as a rough band, and pair it with the patient's own report of whether they feel better
Adopt the largest value so improvements are never overstated
Adopt the smallest value so patients qualify for continued care
Stop using the ODI entirely
items.explanation: The MCID is not a property of the questionnaire — it's a property of the questionnaire PLUS the anchor, population, baseline severity, and statistical method. A range that wide means quoting '6 points' as if it were a physical constant misrepresents the evidence. The patient's global rating of change is the anchor the MCID is trying to approximate; ask them directly.
items.pearl: Anchor-based thresholds describe populations. The person in front of you gets to say whether they're better.
items.citation: Ogura Y, et al. The minimal clinically important difference for the Oswestry Disability Index substantially varies based on calculation method: implications to value-based care. (2024) — see PubMed 38887023.
items.contestedNote: ODI MCID estimates genuinely range from ~1 to >20 points depending on calculation method and population; the commonly quoted 6-point value is one estimate among many.

items.stem: Reported MDC values for the ODI sometimes EXCEED commonly cited MCID values. What does that situation mean in practice?
options: A change can be clinically important yet still fall inside measurement error — you cannot confidently attribute it to real change from one score alone
The MCID must be wrong and should be discarded
It means the measure is unusable
It means any change at all can be treated as real
items.explanation: MDC asks 'is this change bigger than the instrument's noise?'; MCID asks 'is this change big enough to matter to the patient?'. When MDC > MCID, there is an awkward zone where a change matters clinically but can't be distinguished from measurement error in an individual. The response is corroboration — repeat measures over time plus performance measures and the patient's own report — not false precision.
items.citation: Fritz JM, Irrgang JJ. Phys Ther. 2001;81(2):776-788; reported MDC values vary across studies and populations.
items.contestedNote: Published ODI MDC estimates vary substantially (values around 6 and around 12–13 both appear in the literature depending on sample and method). The conceptual point stands regardless of which estimate is used.

items.stem: How does the STarT Back tool assign a patient to the HIGH-risk subgroup?
options: By the psychosocial subscale score (≥4 of the 5 psychosocial items), regardless of total score
By a total score of 9
By any total score of 4 or more
By the presence of referred leg pain
items.explanation: Scoring runs in two stages: a total of 0–3 is low risk; a total ≥4 is then split by the psychosocial subscale — subscale ≤3 is medium risk, subscale ≥4 is high risk. The subscale (bothersomeness, catastrophizing, fear, anxiety, depression) is what separates medium from high, which is precisely why high-risk patients need psychologically informed care rather than simply more of the same.
items.citation: Hill JC, Dunn KM, Lewis M, et al. A primary care back pain screening tool: identifying patient subgroups for initial treatment. Arthritis Rheum. 2008;59(5):632-641.

items.stem: You want to know whether a specific patient can now lift their toddler without a flare — the thing they came to you for. Which measure answers that question most directly?
options: Patient-Specific Functional Scale, with 'lifting my toddler' as a nominated activity
Oswestry Disability Index
Numeric Pain Rating Scale
STarT Back Screening Tool
items.explanation: Each tool answers a different question: the PSFS tracks activities the patient nominates, the ODI tracks standardised disability (and so allows comparison across patients), the NPRS tracks pain intensity, and STarT Back stratifies prognostic risk. For 'can I do MY thing yet', the PSFS is built for it — its weakness, that scores aren't comparable between patients, is irrelevant when tracking one person over time.
items.citation: Horn KK, Jennings S, Richardson G, et al. The Patient-Specific Functional Scale: psychometrics, clinimetrics, and application as a clinical outcome measure. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2012;42(1):30-42.
